# Calibrating LLMs for Text-to-SQL Parsing by Leveraging Sub-clause Frequencies

[All reading notes](../reading-notes.md) · [Catalog entry](../README.md#scf-calibration)

**Full paper read · 2026-11-11**

[Original source](https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-main.859.pdf) · EMNLP 2025 proceedings, pp. 16958–16982, November 4–9, 2025; 25-page published version

**Reading coverage:** All 25 PDF pages: Sections 1–11, Tables 1–17, Figures 1–5 and their captions, Appendix A supplementary experiments and selected cases, Appendix B feature derivation/Algorithms 1–3, and Appendix C prompts, hyperparameters, compute and license statements. Calibration curves (PDF p.8) and Q-MATCH pseudocode (p.22) visually checked. Both pages of the separately linked responsible-research checklist were also read.

**Additional inspected sources:** [Responsible NLP Checklist](https://aclanthology.org/attachments/2025.emnlp-main.859.checklist.pdf)

## Research question

Raw SQL-generation probabilities can be poorly calibrated, limiting their usefulness for identifying likely parser errors.

## Method

SQLGlot-derived clause matches across nucleus and beam candidates yield frequency features for set operations and two query branches. Their products and the primary output’s token-probability score feed a logistic calibration model. The main setup draws ten candidates by each method; calibration changes confidence, not the selected SQL.

## Evaluation

T5-PICARD and Llama models are tested on English Spider/BIRD. Spider development data calibrate the test predictions; BIRD uses 1,000 training examples for calibration and 1,534 development examples for testing. Main results use one calibration run, with ten-bin ECE/ACE, Brier score and error-detection AUC; malformed outputs are removed.

## What the results support

MPS improves all four aggregate metrics over ordinary Platt scaling in the four main model/dataset configurations. Improvements are not uniform within difficulty strata. Smaller calibration samples generally weaken performance, and additional generation adds computational cost.

## Limits and qualifications

Representative labeled calibration data are needed; no distribution-shift or selective-risk guarantee is established. The binary correctness evaluator is not identified precisely enough to call the labels execution-match or test-suite labels. Syntactic agreement is not semantic equivalence. A sensitivity discussion inconsistently describes the default sampling budget, and main metrics lack repeated-run uncertainty.

## Relevance to reliable Text-to-SQL

A practical confidence-calibration baseline for selective SQL answering, distinct from detecting an unanswerable request or validating the user’s intended interpretation.

## Checks against the paper

These are interpretations checked against the source, not verbatim quotations attributed to its authors.

| Claim or inference examined | Original evidence | Location | Assessment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Better calibration certifies correct admitted SQL or a guaranteed abstention risk. | The objective is binwise average correctness under distribution D; experiments report calibration metrics and AUC, without a selective-risk theorem or an evaluated answer/abstain policy. | Section 3, Equations 1–3; Sections 5.4 and 6.2; Table 1 | Use as empirical confidence/error-ranking evidence under the tested distributions, not an individual-query or abstention guarantee. |
| The evaluated correctness labels are fully specified execution labels over every generated query. | Section 3 defines Y as correctness relative to the prompt; Sections 5 and Appendix A/Table 5 do not name an execution-match, exact-match or test-suite labeling procedure. Section 5.3 excludes some syntactically erroneous outputs. | Section 3; Sections 5.1–5.4; Appendix A, Accuracy of language models/Table 5 | Keep the correctness-oracle uncertainty and syntactic filtering explicit; do not infer a concrete evaluator or full-output-population result. |
| The main method uses only five candidates per sampling scheme. | Section 5.3, Appendix A/Table 5 and Appendix C.2 specify ten nucleus plus ten beam candidates. Section 7.4/Table 3 legitimately varies k, but its prose calls k=5 the setting used in the paper. | Sections 5.3 and 7.4/Table 3; Appendix A/Table 5; Appendix C.2 | Use the consistently specified main budget of 20 candidates. Treat the sensitivity discussion’s default-setting phrase as a reporting inconsistency, not evidence that the sensitivity experiment is invalid. |
